title: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
summary: Why pointer chasing and streaming hit different memory walls, how Little's law links bandwidth to misses in flight, how hardware and software prefetching hide latency, and when streaming stores save bandwidth.
outcomes: Explain why a dependent pointer chase is latency-bound while an array scan is bandwidth-bound
Compute single-core bandwidth from latency and lines in flight with Little's law
Predict where hardware prefetchers succeed and fail, including at 4 KB page boundaries
Choose a software prefetch distance from miss latency and work per iteration, and spot harmful prefetches
Decide when non-temporal stores cut memory traffic and when they make things worse

lessons.title: Latency versus bandwidth: two different walls

blocks.md:
Recall from the cache hierarchy course: data moves between memory and the CPU in 64-byte **cache lines**, and an access that misses every cache level has to wait for main memory. This course is about what that wait costs and how to hide it.

Two words describe a memory system. **Latency** is the time from issuing one load until its data arrives (measured in nanoseconds or CPU cycles). **Bandwidth** is how many bytes per second the memory system can deliver when it is kept busy. They are different limits, and code usually runs into only one of them at a time.

blocks.caption: Both loops read every element once. Only loop A lets the hardware know the next address before the current load finishes.

blocks.md:
In loop A the address of `a[i+1]` is `a + i + 1`, computable right now. The CPU and its prefetchers can request many future lines at once, so the loop is limited by how fast bytes arrive: it is **bandwidth-bound**.

In loop B the address of the next node is the value being loaded. Nothing can start until the current load returns, so each node pays a full memory round trip. That loop is **latency-bound**.

blocks.prompt: Ulrich Drepper timed a list walk on a Pentium 4 whose main memory takes 200 to 300 cycles per access. The nodes were 8 bytes and the working set far bigger than the 1 MB L2. Layout 1: nodes in address order. Layout 2: same nodes, random order. Guess cycles per node for each.
blocks.reveal:
**Sequential layout: about 9 cycles per node. Random layout: 450 cycles and more.**

Both programs follow pointers, but in the sequential layout the next node is in the same or the next cache line, so the hardware prefetcher already has the line on its way. In the random layout every node is a fresh miss, plus TLB misses for address translation. Drepper notes the hardware prefetching even works against the random case, pushing it above the raw memory latency.

blocks.title: Cycles per list node on a Pentium 4 (Drepper, 2007)

scenes.caption: Reference latencies on this machine: an L1d hit costs about 4 cycles, an L2 access about 14, and main memory 200 to 300 (the low end, 200, is shown). The two walks are not run yet.
Sequential walk with a working set far beyond L2: about 9 cycles per node, cheaper than even one L2 access. The prefetcher fetched each line before the loop asked for it.
Same walk with nodes in random order: 450 cycles and more. No pattern to detect, so every node waits for a full miss plus address translation. Same instructions, about 50 times slower.

blocks.md: **The one thing to remember:** ask whether the next address is known before the current load finishes. If not, you are latency-bound and more bandwidth will not help. If yes, you are probably bandwidth-bound and the question becomes how many bytes you move.

Common misconception: "faster RAM will speed up my tree or hash-chain lookups." Faster transfer rates raise peak bandwidth, but a dependent chain of misses uses a tiny fraction of it. Its cost is set by latency, which has improved far more slowly.

blocks.question: Which workload is most likely latency-bound once its data is far larger than the caches?
options: Summing a large float array
Copying a 2 GB buffer with memcpy
Descending a pointer-based binary search tree with random keys
Adding two large vectors element by element
blocks.explain: Each tree level's child pointer comes from the node just loaded, so misses happen one after another. The other three compute every address from a loop index, so many lines can be requested in parallel and the limit is bytes per second.

blocks.question: Drepper's random list walk cost more cycles per node (450+) than the machine's raw memory latency (200 to 300). Which explanation matches Drepper's measurements?
options: The random walk executes more instructions per node
Every node also needs an address translation (TLB miss), and the hardware prefetcher wastes effort on useless lines
Random addresses bypass the cache entirely
The CPU runs at a lower clock speed during random access
blocks.explain: The loop body is identical in both layouts. Drepper attributes the extra cost to TLB misses, which add translation time to each access, and to automatic prefetching that works to a disadvantage when the pattern is random.

lessons.title: Little's law: how many misses must be in flight

blocks.md: A modern out-of-order core does not have to wait for one miss before issuing the next, as long as the addresses are independent. Each outstanding L1 miss occupies a **fill buffer** (Intel's name for the slot that tracks a line on its way in). Intel's optimization manual lists 16 fill buffers for its Golden Cove cores. The L2 has its own, deeper miss queues (48 entries on Golden Cove).

How much bandwidth do you get from a given number of misses in flight? Queueing theory answers with **Little's law**: the average number of items inside a system equals arrival rate times time spent inside. David Bailey's note applies it to memory, in a form Bailey credits to Burton Smith: concurrency equals bandwidth times latency.

blocks.caption: C is the number of cache lines in flight, B the bandwidth, L the latency of one miss. The right form counts C in 64-byte lines.

blocks.md:
Worked example on a **model machine** (round numbers chosen for clarity, not a specific CPU): memory latency $L = 80$ ns, 64-byte lines.

- One miss at a time: $64 / 80 = 0.8$ GB/s.
- 10 lines in flight: $10 \times 64 / 80 = 8.0$ GB/s.
- 16 lines in flight (one core's fill buffers): $12.8$ GB/s.

Bandwidth grows linearly with concurrency until something else saturates, such as the DRAM channels.

scenes.caption: Pointer chasing: line 1's address is inside line 0, so each 80 ns miss starts only when the previous one ends. 4 lines take 320 ns: 0.8 GB/s.
Array walk: all four addresses are known, so the core issues one miss per ns and they overlap. Done at 83 ns: 3.08 GB/s, almost 4 times the serial rate (simplified: one issue per ns).

blocks.prompt: Same model: latency 80 ns, 64-byte lines. Suppose the DRAM can deliver 40 GB/s. How many lines must be in flight to reach that peak, and can one core with 16 fill buffers do it from L1 misses alone?
blocks.reveal:
$C = B \times L / 64 = 40 \times 80 / 64 = 50$ lines. Sixteen fill buffers give at most $12.8$ GB/s, about a third of peak.

This is why L2 hardware prefetchers matter for bandwidth: they issue requests from the L2's deeper miss queues, adding concurrency beyond what the core's own demand loads can hold. It is also why a single thread often cannot saturate a memory system that many threads together can.

blocks.title: Bandwidth from lines in flight (Little's law)

scenes.caption: Model: 80 ns latency, 40 GB/s peak. Bandwidth climbs by 0.8 GB/s per extra line in flight and flattens at 50 lines. At 16 lines a core reaches 12.8 GB/s.
Raise latency to 120 ns (a busier or remote memory node) with the same peak. The same 16 lines now give only 8.53 GB/s: higher latency directly cuts single-core bandwidth.
Raise the peak to 80 GB/s at 80 ns. The 16-line point does not move at all: buying faster DRAM does nothing for code that cannot keep more lines in flight.

blocks.md: **Prefetching is a way to raise concurrency.** A prefetch is a miss started early, before the program's own load. Anything that lets more independent misses overlap (prefetchers, unrolled loops, several independent lists walked at once, more threads) moves you up the curve.

blocks.question: A core keeps 16 lines in flight and memory latency rises from 80 ns to 120 ns. Peak DRAM bandwidth is not the limit. What happens to this core's bandwidth?
options: It stays at 12.8 GB/s because peak bandwidth did not change
It drops to about 8.5 GB/s
It rises, because longer latency means more lines are in flight
It drops to 0.8 GB/s
blocks.explain: With concurrency capped at 16 lines, $B = 16 \times 64 / 120 \approx 8.53$ GB/s. Little's law says bandwidth is concurrency divided by latency, so longer latency at fixed concurrency means less bandwidth.

blocks.question: You move a linked-list walk to a CPU with twice as many fill buffers. The list nodes are in random order. Roughly how does the walk's speed change?
options: About the same
About 2 times faster
About half as fast
Faster only if the list fits in L1
blocks.explain: A single pointer chase has concurrency 1: the next address is unknown until the current miss returns. Extra fill buffers sit empty. To benefit you would need several independent chains walked at the same time.

lessons.title: Hardware prefetchers: patterns, training and the page wall

blocks.md: A **hardware prefetcher** is logic in the cache that watches miss addresses and requests lines it predicts you will need. Drepper describes the trigger: usually a sequence of **two or more misses** in a recognizable pattern, to adjacent lines or with a fixed stride. One miss is not enough, because isolated misses (globals, hash lookups) are common and prefetching after each would mostly waste bandwidth.

blocks.title: Where the prefetchers sit (Intel, as documented)

nodes.label:
L1 prefetchers
next line, IP stride

scenes.caption: Demand loads flow from the core through L1 and L2 to DRAM. Each miss level is watched by its own prefetch logic.

The IP-based stride prefetcher keys on the address of the load instruction, so it can spot a fixed stride per load even when several loads interleave. Intel notes it uses only the low 8 bits of that address.

The L2 streamer and data prefetch logic (DPL) fetch from DRAM into L2. On Intel Core they trigger only for normal write-back memory and stay inside one 4 KB page. L1 prefetches and software prefetches can trigger them too.

blocks.md: Classic prefetchers do not cross page boundaries. Intel's manual states its hardware prefetcher will not prefetch across a 4 KB page boundary; a demand load must touch the new page first. Drepper gives the reason: the next virtual page might be unmapped or swapped out, and a prefetch that caused a page fault would be a fault the program never asked for. So every new page costs at least one ordinary miss before the prefetcher can retrain. Newer cores soften this: the same manual describes a next-page prefetcher, and Redwood Cove's LLC page prefetcher fetches two pages ahead, so measure on your target.

blocks.title: A stream through two pages (simplified to 8 lines per page)

scenes.caption: The loop reads line A0: a miss. One miss is not a pattern, so nothing else is fetched. (Simplified: a real 4 KB page holds 64 lines, not 8.)
A1 also misses. Two misses to consecutive lines: the prefetcher now has a pattern and starts requesting ahead.
Steady state: the prefetcher stays ahead (Intel describes two lines ahead for its last-level prefetcher). Loads of A2 to A5 find their lines already arriving.
At A7 the next lines B0 and B1 are on a different page. The prefetcher stops at the boundary instead of risking a fault.
B0 and B1 are ordinary misses again; only after them does the prefetcher retrain and run ahead to B2 and B3. Every page pays this startup cost.

blocks.prompt: You loop over an array of 4096-byte records and read only one 8-byte field from each. Will the hardware prefetcher hide the misses once the array is much bigger than the caches?
blocks.reveal: **Mostly no.** Each access lands on a new 4 KB page, and the classic stream and stride prefetchers never cross a page, so there is never a second miss on the same page to train on. Intel adds that constant strides only work when the stride is under half the prefetcher's trigger distance, and Drepper cites a stride-detection window of about 512 bytes as common. Fix the layout instead: put the hot field of every record into its own dense array.

blocks.md: Two more documented costs. First, a startup penalty: the prefetcher needs a couple of misses before it starts, which hurts short arrays. Second, it overshoots: it requests lines past the end of an array that are never used, wasting bandwidth. And it mostly recognizes linear patterns; Drepper (2007) notes prefetch units then did not attempt non-linear ones, which are usually random anyway. Newer cores add a few special cases, such as Redwood Cove's array-of-pointers prefetcher.

Hardware prefetching is not free: every useless prefetch costs memory bandwidth and can evict a line you still needed. That is how it can make a random walk slower than raw memory latency. Drepper describes Intel's model-specific register switch for disabling it (bit 9 of IA32_MISC_ENABLE on many processors of that time) for workloads that measurably suffer.

blocks.question: You process particles in a loop and read only `x`, `y`, `z` of each. Which layout gives the hardware prefetcher the easiest job once the data exceeds the caches?
options: An array of 256-byte particle structs, reading three fields per struct
Separate dense arrays `x[]`, `y[]`, `z[]`
A linked list of particle structs allocated in loop order
A hash map from particle id to struct
blocks.explain: Dense arrays give three unit-stride streams where every byte fetched is used. The 256-byte structs also form a stride, but each 64-byte line fetched carries only the three fields you read (24 bytes if they are doubles), so most bytes moved are wasted. The list and hash map add dependent or scattered addresses.

blocks.question: A loop reads two cache lines sequentially, then jumps to a random place and reads two lines again, and so on. Why does the hardware prefetcher help very little here?
options: Prefetchers only work on writes
The prefetcher requires 64 consecutive lines before starting
Random jumps disable the cache
After the two misses that train it, the stream ends, so its predictions point at lines that will never be read
blocks.explain: Training takes about two misses, and by then this short run is over. The prefetcher's guesses past the end become wasted bandwidth, the same overshoot Intel's manual warns about for short arrays.

lessons.title: Software prefetch: distance, hints and the kernel's lesson

blocks.md: When the pattern is irregular but you can compute future addresses, you can issue the prefetch yourself. GCC and Clang expose `__builtin_prefetch(addr, rw, locality)`. `rw` is 0 for a read (the default), 1 for a write, or 2 for a shared read in recent GCC. `locality` runs from 0 (no temporal locality, no need to keep it) to 3 (keep it in all cache levels, the default). If the target has prefetch instructions GCC emits them; otherwise it emits nothing.

On x86 the intrinsic `_mm_prefetch(p, hint)` maps to `prefetcht0`, `prefetcht1`, `prefetcht2` and `prefetchnta`. Intel's table for Skylake: T0 fills L1 and L2, T1 and T2 fill L2 but not L1, NTA fills L1 but not L2. Intel stresses these hints are implementation specific, so measure on your target.

A prefetch is only a hint. It does not change program results, and GCC documents that it does not fault on an invalid address. It still has a cost: Intel says a prefetch to an unmapped address, such as NULL, can cause long delays.

The key tuning knob is the **prefetch distance** $d$: how many iterations ahead you prefetch. Too short and the data is still in flight when you need it. Too long and it may be evicted before use. If one iteration takes $W$ cycles of work and a miss takes $L$ cycles, the prefetch must be issued at least $L$ cycles early.

blocks.caption: Simplified model: it assumes enough fill buffers for d misses in flight and that prefetched lines are not evicted early.

blocks.title: Time per iteration versus prefetch distance

scenes.caption: Model: L = 300 cycles, W = 40. With d = 1 each iteration waits 300 cycles; d = 2 gives 150, d = 4 gives 75. From d = 8 on, the miss is fully hidden and the loop runs at 40 cycles per iteration.
Cheaper work per iteration (W = 20) means you must look further ahead: the knee moves to d = 15. Small loop bodies need large distances.
Heavy work per iteration (W = 160) hides most of the latency by itself: d = 2 is already enough. Large loop bodies can prefetch just one or two iterations ahead.

blocks.md: Software prefetch shines on **indirect access**, where addresses come from an index array. The hardware prefetcher sees random lines in `table`, but the program can read `idx[i + d]` early because `idx` itself streams sequentially.

blocks.title: Prefetching a gather loop with distance 8

scenes.caption: Iteration 0. The prefetch requests the table line needed 8 iterations from now. The load of table[idx[0]] itself still misses: nothing prefetched it.
Iterations 0 to 7 only warm the pipeline. Their loads miss, but each one also launched a future prefetch, so up to 8 misses overlap.
Iteration 8: the line for table[idx[8]] was requested during iteration 0. If 8 iterations take longer than one miss, it has arrived and this load hits.
Near the end the guard stops prefetching past the array. Without it, idx[i + D] would read beyond idx: the prefetch never faults, but that out-of-bounds read of idx is ordinary code and can fault.

blocks.md: GCC's docs make the subtle point in the last scene: the prefetch instruction never faults, but the **address expression** is ordinary code. Prefetching `p->next` is safe even if `p->next` is garbage; evaluating it when `p` itself is invalid crashes.

Linked lists are the hard case: to prefetch the node 5 hops ahead you must already have walked there. Drepper's test could prefetch 5 list elements ahead (each node took about 160 cycles of work, and by Drepper's count two cache lines had to be prefetched per node). Beyond the 512 KB L2, prefetching saved 50 to 60 cycles per node, up to 8%, and cost nothing measurable when the data fit in cache.

The Linux kernel learned the other side. Its list macros prefetched `pos->next` on every step. In 2011 Linus Torvalds found those prefetches at the top of a kernel-build profile; Ingo Molnar measured about a 0.5% loss and about 20 cycles for each prefetch of the NULL pointer that ends a list. The hardware prefetcher was already issuing about the same number of prefetches, so the prefetches were removed from the list traversals.

**Rule:** add a software prefetch only where profiling shows misses, one site at a time, and keep it only if performance counters show useful prefetches and the timing improves. Drepper and the kernel developers reached the same conclusion from opposite results.

blocks.question: A loop does about 30 cycles of work per iteration and each miss costs about 250 cycles. Using the simple model, what is the smallest prefetch distance that hides the miss?
blocks.explain: $d \ge \lceil 250 / 30 \rceil = \lceil 8.33 \rceil = 9$. With d = 8 the prefetch is issued only 240 cycles ahead, 10 cycles short, so the miss is not fully hidden: the model gives $\max(30, 250/8) = 31.25$ cycles per iteration instead of 30.

blocks.question: Spot the problem: `for (p = head; p; p = p->next) { __builtin_prefetch(p->next); work(p); }` on a list of 3 nodes that is walked millions of times.
options: It can crash when p->next is NULL
The prefetch needs locality 0 to be legal
Nothing: the hardware ignores prefetches of NULL at no cost
Distance 1 is too short to hide a miss behind `work`, and on every walk the last prefetch targets NULL, which Intel says can cause long delays
blocks.explain: This is the kernel's list pattern. A prefetch never faults, so there is no crash, but one hop ahead hides little latency on a short list, and the NULL prefetch at the end of every walk was measured at about 20 cycles. The kernel removed these prefetches.

lessons.title: Bandwidth-bound code: count the bytes, skip the reads

blocks.md: Once enough misses are in flight, a streaming loop hits the other wall: bytes per second. Then the only lever is to **move fewer bytes**. A hidden source of extra bytes is the store. Writing to normal (write-back) memory first reads the whole line into the cache, called a **read for ownership** (RFO), then modifies it, then later writes it back. Writing a large buffer that you never read still reads it.

scenes.caption: Ordinary stores: the destination is read before it is overwritten, so a 1 GB copy moves 3 GB. At a model 20 GB/s that is 150 ms.
Non-temporal stores write full lines straight to memory with no RFO: 2 GB moved, 100 ms at the same 20 GB/s. A third less time for a bandwidth-bound copy (simplified: ignores other traffic).

blocks.md:
**Non-temporal** (streaming) stores, such as `_mm_stream_si128` (the `movntdq` instruction), tell the CPU the data will not be reused soon. Intel lists two benefits: no RFO bus requests when all 64 bytes of a line are written consecutively and combined into one write, and less eviction of useful cached data.

The rules: write each line completely and back to back so the write-combining buffer can merge it, and because these stores are weakly ordered, issue an `sfence` before another thread or device relies on the data.

blocks.caption: Adapted from Drepper's setbytes example: four back-to-back 16-byte streaming stores fill one whole line, so write combining emits a single 64-byte write with no read.

blocks.prompt: Drepper initialized a 3000 by 3000 matrix of 4-byte values (36 MB) four ways: normal or non-temporal stores, walking along rows (sequential) or down columns. Predict which combination is slowest.
blocks.reveal: Non-temporal stores down columns: 0.160 s (about 225 MB/s). Along rows, non-temporal stores tied normal stores at 0.048 s (750 MB/s). Down columns, normal stores took 0.127 s (283 MB/s), but non-temporal ones could not combine anything: each 4-byte store became its own memory write. Streaming stores pay off only when you write whole lines in order.

scenes.caption: Normal stores: sequential rows reach 750 MB/s; column order drops to 283 MB/s because consecutive stores land in different cache lines.

Non-temporal stores match the cached run in row order thanks to write combining, and fall to 225 MB/s in column order where no combining is possible. (Measured on 2007 hardware; the ratios are the lesson.)

blocks.md: Do not sprinkle streaming stores everywhere. Intel recommends them for memset-style fills larger than about half the last-level cache when the data is not read soon after. On Skylake server it warns that overusing them on smaller blocks evicts lines you need and can hit a per-core limit on non-temporal write bandwidth.
Putting the course together: first find which wall you are hitting, then pick the matching fix.

scenes.caption: Start from a profile showing memory stalls. The first question is about dependence, not size: does each address come out of the previous load?
Yes: a pointer chase is latency-bound. Bandwidth is idle. Shrink and densify nodes, walk several independent chains together, or prefetch when you can know addresses ahead.
No, addresses are known: measure achieved bandwidth. Near the DRAM peak means bandwidth-bound: move fewer bytes. Far below means too few misses in flight: unroll, add threads, or software prefetch.

blocks.question: A single-threaded loop streams through a 4 GB array and achieves 11 GB/s on a server whose memory system delivers 150 GB/s across all cores. Adding software prefetches does not help. What is the most promising next step?
options: Switch to non-temporal stores, since it must be bandwidth-bound
Convert the array to a linked list
Split the work across several threads so more lines are in flight in total
Disable the hardware prefetcher
blocks.explain: 11 of 150 GB/s is far from peak, so this is not the bandwidth wall. A single core's concurrency (fill buffers plus L2 queues) caps it, as Little's law predicts. More cores bring more miss slots. Non-temporal stores reduce bytes, which matters only near the peak.

blocks.question: A function zeroes a 256 MB buffer that will be filled with new data by a different stage minutes later. The machine has a 32 MB last-level cache. What does switching from ordinary stores to full-line non-temporal stores mainly save?
options: The read for ownership of every destination line, and the eviction of useful cached data
Nothing, because stores never read memory
The final sfence
Address translation for each page
blocks.explain: Ordinary stores read each line before overwriting it (RFO), so zeroing moves about twice the bytes. Full-line streaming stores skip that read and avoid flushing the cache with 256 MB of data nobody needs soon. This matches Intel's guidance for fills larger than half the LLC.
